slides.title: Reading the Economy: CPI, GDP and Jobs
lines: How economic releases become market surprises, not misleading headlines.
A NUMBER IS NOT ITS INTERPRETATION.
Read the unit, comparison, revisions, market benchmark and timing before the reaction.

slides.title: Why can “good” data trigger a selloff?
lines: “GDP beat expectations. Why are stocks falling?”
Prices react to the surprise and its effect on policy, valuation and prior positioning.

slides.title: Five questions before reading any economic headline
lines: Never substitute a forecast from after publication for pre-release consensus.

slides.title: CPI and PCE measure different things
lines: BLS consumer price basket; household spending focus.
BEA wider personal consumption coverage and different weighting.
Usually strips food and energy; persistence lens, not total cost of living.
Headline and core can move in opposite directions. Check which is being quoted.

slides.title: One monthly increase does not equal the annual rate
lines: Illustrative constant +0.3% monthly; historical YoY depends on the actual prior 12 months.
MoM, YoY and annualised rates answer different questions.

slides.title: A falling YoY rate need not mean prices fall
lines: Current prices may still rise, just more slowly than the same month a year earlier.
Deflation means the relevant price index itself declines, not merely a lower inflation rate.

slides.title: GDP reports are usually annualised
lines: Illustrative 4% SAAR. Real strips inflation; nominal does not.
US GDP advance, second and third estimates use improving information.

slides.title: A strong headline can hide a weak domestic story
lines: Household demand and real income durability.
Business fixed spending, housing, inventory swing.
Imports subtract in the expenditure identity; interpret with consumption and inventory.
Track final sales to private domestic purchasers, not headline GDP alone.

slides.title: Why jobs growth and unemployment may disagree
lines: Nonfarm payrolls measure jobs at businesses and other establishments.
Unemployment and labour participation are derived from people/household survey.
Different populations, samples and sampling errors; not proof one is fake.

slides.title: The payroll headline is not the labour market
lines: Have the prior two months been revised?
Is unemployment rising because more people seek jobs?
Are average hours and hourly earnings cooling?
Are jobs concentrated in a few industries?

slides.title: A real economic calendar needs these columns
lines: The original prior release, and revised value.
Exact agency measure, unit and release time.
How 2Y/10Y, DXY, gold and equity prices reacted.
A “beat” is a statistical comparison, not a guaranteed bullish trade.

slides.title: Map the plausible policy transmission
lines: Gold and oil can add contradictory signals; test rather than force an explanation.

slides.title: The release may not explain the entire session
lines: Best for immediate announcement repricing, provided prices/quotes are matched.
Also contains other events, positioning, opening gaps and late commentary.
Use “followed” rather than “caused” when mechanism evidence is missing.

slides.title: Three arithmetic and method checks
lines: +0.3% MoM annualised at same monthly rate?
4% real GDP SAAR means actual q/q growth?
Where does US unemployment rate come from?
Challenge: can a data beat still be dovish relative to priced expectations? Yes.
